This analysis estimates what the home is worth in today's market, recommends a list price, and shows what each pricing choice is likely to net you.

recommendation.paragraph: Recent sales of similar Spring Oaks pool homes, adjusted for their differences from yours, support a value of roughly $455,000 to $480,000. We recommend launching at $469,900, the middle of what those sales support. It leaves room for the negotiating that is normal right now, and it presents the home as fairly priced during its first few weeks on the market, when buyer attention is highest. The two sales that would support a higher price closed in the spring, when mortgage rates were lower and homes sold faster than they do now.

means: Expect to negotiate. Homes nearby that sold since July closed at about 95.2% of their original asking price, and nearly nine in ten sellers paid part of the buyer's closing costs, typically about $12,000. A likely sale price at $469,900 is in the low-to-mid $460,000s.

The first three weeks matter most. A new listing gets its biggest wave of showings right away. If it is priced where buyers expect, that wave turns into offers; if not, the home starts to look stale and the price cut comes later, from a weaker position.
Watch the appraisal. Only two Spring Oaks homes of similar size have sold above $480,000, both in the spring. A contract well above that level would risk a low appraisal and a renegotiation.

Documentation is worth money. Your updates are the reason this home can sell near the top of the neighborhood. Permits and dates for the roof and the renovation turn them from claims into value a buyer and an appraiser can rely on.

comps.intro: We looked at every sale within one mile since April 2026 and chose the five closest matches: Spring Oaks pool homes of about 1,800–1,900 square feet, built in the 1970s. Each is adjusted for its differences from your home, so it reflects what that home would have sold for if it were yours.
comps.method_note: Adjustments used: about $75 per square foot of size difference; $30,000–$45,000 for a home that hadn't been renovated to this level; $5,000–$10,000 for a noticeably larger or better lot; 1–2% off spring sales because prices have softened since. Seller-paid costs are subtracted from the sale price, since they reduce what the seller actually received. Condition adjustments are based on listing descriptions, not visits, so they are judgment calls.

comps.summary_paragraph: The adjusted values run from about $436,000 to $492,000, with a median of $469,800. The two highest are the closest matches to your home's condition but sold in a stronger spring market; the two lowest needed the largest adjustments. Other Spring Oaks sales support the same picture: 607 Green Briar Blvd (a 2014 renovation, pool) sold for $427,000 in April, and 623 Lakespur Ln (renovated, no pool) sold for $435,000 in May.

market.intro: We looked at 33 sales within one mile of this home between April and mid-September 2026. The market has cooled noticeably since spring.
rows: Typical sale vs. original asking price
Typical days to go under contract
bullets: Buyers are negotiating again. Since July, homes nearby sold for about 5% under their original asking price and took almost three times as long to go under contract as in the spring.
Inventory is balanced. There are 15 other homes for sale nearby, about four months of supply at the summer pace, and more than half have already cut their price.
Mortgage rates are up. The 30-year average was 6.95% the week of September 17, versus roughly 6.2–6.4% during the spring sales. Buyers' budgets stretch less than they did in April.
Timing. Fewer buyers shop between Thanksgiving and New Year's. Launching in the next few weeks gives the home its best window before the holidays.

pricing.intro: Three realistic options. Expected sale prices and timelines are our estimates from recent sales, not guarantees. All three are likely to net within a few thousand dollars of each other, so the real difference is time and risk.

strategies.note: Tests the top of the range; likely needs a price cut before an offer

strategies.note: Priced at the middle of recent adjusted sales; room to negotiate

pricing.note: The $459,900 option assumes a smaller seller credit ($5,000) because competing offers usually ask for less help; if they don't materialize, its net falls to about the others' level or below.
pricing.net_intro: What each option is likely to leave you after the costs a Florida seller typically pays at closing.
pricing.net_note: Not included: your mortgage payoff, your share of this year's property taxes (about $228 for each month of the year before closing, credited to the buyer), and any repairs agreed after inspection. While the home is on the market you keep paying the mortgage, taxes, insurance, and utilities, which is the real cost of a slower strategy.

buyer_payment.note: Conventional loan, 5% down, 6.95% 30-year fixed (Freddie Mac average, week of September 17, 2026), Altamonte Springs property taxes with homestead, $3,600 a year insurance (placeholder), and 0.5% mortgage insurance.

prep.intro: These steps cost little and remove the questions that slow Florida buyers down or cost sellers money at the negotiating table.
items: Document the roof. Have the permit and completion date ready to share. Roof age decides whether a buyer can insure the home, so a documented new roof is one of the most valuable facts in the listing.
Get a pre-listing inspection, 4-point, and wind-mitigation report. Buyers can get insurance quotes before they offer, and you learn about any issue before a buyer uses it to renegotiate.
Gather the renovation permits. Kitchen, bath, electrical, and plumbing work. Unpermitted work can surface during the buyer's due diligence and delay or derail a sale.
Check the public record. Make sure the property appraiser's record matches the four bedrooms and two baths we will advertise.
Make it easy to show. Lockbox access through the standard showing system with short notice gets the most buyers through in the first weeks.
Decide on a seller-credit budget now. Most recent sales included one. A credit toward a temporary rate buydown lowers a buyer's payment far more in the first years than the same amount off the price.
Agree on a review point. If there are steady showings but no offer after about three weeks, we revisit the price with fresh data rather than waiting.

needs: The roof permit and replacement date, plus any existing 4-point or wind-mitigation report.
The age of the AC, water heater, and pool equipment, and the dates of the kitchen, bath, and flooring work.
The electrical panel brand, whether the home has aluminum branch wiring, and whether the plumbing has been updated. Both are common questions for homes built in the early 1970s.
Copies of any permits for the renovation work.
Anything you know that affects the home's value or condition, such as past leaks, insurance claims, or repairs. Florida law requires sellers to disclose known material defects.
Your estimated mortgage payoff, so we can turn the net estimates into cash at closing.
When you would like to close, and whether the home will be occupied or vacant during showings.
method: This analysis uses the property details and current tax bill you provided; a Stellar MLS search of single-family homes within one mile (sales from April 6 to September 17, 2026, plus current active, pending, and expired listings); and the Freddie Mac weekly mortgage rate survey for September 17, 2026. Florida documentary stamp tax and owner's title insurance are calculated at the state's standard rates.

This is a broker's opinion of value based on comparable sales. It is not an appraisal. Expected sale prices, timelines, costs, and net proceeds are estimates for planning, not guarantees; your closing agent will provide exact figures. Condition adjustments are based on listing descriptions of the comparable homes and on the updates you described, and will be refined once we see your records. Market conditions change, so this analysis should be refreshed if the home is not listed within a few weeks.
